title: De Carnis Resurrectione
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa026.opp-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: At ego magis ridebo vulgus, tunc quoque, cum ipsos defunctos atrocissime exurit, quos postmodum gulosissime nutrit, isdem ignibus et promerens et offendens. O pietatem de crudelitate ludentem! Sacrificat an insultat, cum crematis cremat? Plane cum vulgo interdum et sapientes sententiam suam iungunt. Nihil esse post mortem Epicuri schola est. Ait et Seneca omnia post mortem finiri, etiam ipsam. Satis est autem si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedoclis et Platonici immortalem animam e contrario reclamant, immo adhuc proxime etiam in corpora remeabilem affirmant, etsi non in eadem, etsi non in humana tantummodo, ut Euphorbus in Pythagoram, Homerus in pavum recenseantur.
passages.english: But I will laugh at the common crowd all the more, even at the moment when they burn the dead themselves most savagely, whom they afterwards feed most gluttonously, both earning their favour and offending them with the same fires. O piety that makes sport out of cruelty! Is it sacrificing or insulting, when it burns [offerings] to the burned? Indeed, sometimes even the wise join their opinion to the crowd's. That there is nothing after death is the teaching of Epicurus' school. Seneca too says that everything is ended after death, even [death] itself. It is enough, however, that the no lesser philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles and the Platonists cries out to the contrary that the soul is immortal, and indeed goes still closer, affirming that it can even return into bodies, though not into the same ones, and not only into human ones, so that Euphorbus is reckoned [to have come back] in Pythagoras, and Homer in a peacock.
passages.notes: "Sacrificat an insultat, cum crematis cremat?": the object of the second cremat is unexpressed, presumably the offerings burned for the dead; the phrasing is a deliberate wordplay. "etiam ipsam" probably refers to death itself (mors); some take it as the soul, but the feminine fits mortem.

passages.original: Nulli denique alii salutem corporali substantiae invident quam alterius divinitatis haeretici. Ideoque et Christum aliter disponere coacti, ne creatoris habeatur, in ipsa prius carne eius erraverunt, aut nullius veritatis contendentes eam secundum Marcionem et Basiliden, aut propriae qualitatis secundum haereses Valentini et Apellen. Atque ita sequitur ut salutem eius substantiae excludant cuius Christum consortem negant, certi illam summo praeiudicio resurrectionis instructam, si iam in Christo resurrexit caro.
passages.english: In short, no others begrudge salvation to the bodily substance than the heretics of another divinity. And therefore, being compelled also to arrange Christ differently, so that he may not be held to belong to the Creator, they first went astray concerning his very flesh, contending either that it had no reality, according to Marcion and Basilides, or that it was of a peculiar quality, according to the heresies of Valentinus and Apelles. And so it follows that they exclude the salvation of that substance of which they deny Christ was a sharer, being certain that it is furnished with the highest prejudgment of resurrection if the flesh has already risen in Christ.
passages.notes: "Summo praeiudicio": i.e. the strongest precedent or presumption in favour of the resurrection; "praeiudicium" is a legal term for a prior ruling that settles a case in advance.

passages.original: Animae autem salutem credo retractatu carere. Omnes enim fere haeretici eam quoquo modo volunt, tamen non negant. Viderit unus aliqui Lucanus, nec huic quidem substantiae parcens, quam secundum Aristotelem dissolvens aliud quid pro ea subicit, tertium quiddam resurrecturus, neque anima neque caro, id est non homo, sed ursus forsitan, qua Lucanus. Habet et iste a nobis plenissimum de omni statu animae stilum, quam inprimis immortalem tuentes solius carnis et defectionem agnoscimus et refectionem cum maxime adserimus, redactis in ordinarium materiae corpus, si qua et alibi pro causarum incursione praestricta distulimus.
passages.english: The salvation of the soul, however, I believe needs no discussion. For almost all the heretics, in whatever way they conceive it, still do not deny it. Let one particular Lucanus see to himself, who does not spare even this substance, but, dissolving it in Aristotle's manner, substitutes something else for it, so that he will rise as some third thing, neither soul nor flesh, that is, not a man, but perhaps a bear, as being Lucanus. He too has from us a very full treatise on every condition of the soul, which we maintain first of all to be immortal, while we acknowledge the failing of the flesh alone and most emphatically assert its restoration, bringing back into the regular body of the subject-matter whatever points we have elsewhere touched on briefly and put off, as the cases arising required.
passages.notes: "qua Lucanus": a pun on Lucanus and the Lucanian ox (Luca bos, i.e. elephant) or a Lucanian beast; the joke's exact point is uncertain. Lucanus is a Marcionite heretic. "stilum" refers to Tertullian's De Anima.

passages.original: Igitur quoniam et rudes quique de communibus adhuc sensibus sapiunt, et dubii et simplices per eosdem sensus denuo inquietantur, et ubique primus iste in nos aries temperatur quo carnis condicio quassatur, necessario et a nobis carnis primum condicio munietur, vituperatione laudatione depulsa. Ita nos rhetoricari quoque provocant haeretici, sicut etiam philosophari. Futile et frivolum istud corpusculum, quod malum denique appellare non horrent, etsi angelorum fuisset operatio, ut Menandro et Marco placet, etsi ignei alicuius exstructio aeque angeli, ut Apelles docet, sufficeret ad auctoritatem carnis secundae divinitatis patrocinium. Angelos post deum novimus. Iam nunc quisquis ille summus deus haeretici cuiusque est, non immerito ab ipso quoque deducerem carnis dignitatem, a quo voluntas producendae ei adfuisset.
passages.english: Therefore, since all the uninstructed still think according to common perceptions, and the doubtful and the simple are unsettled afresh through those same perceptions, and everywhere this battering-ram is first brought to bear against us, by which the condition of the flesh is shaken, we too must of necessity first fortify the condition of the flesh, repelling disparagement with praise. Thus the heretics provoke us to play the rhetorician too, just as [they provoke us] to play the philosopher. This futile and trifling little body, which in the end they do not shrink from calling evil, even if it had been the work of angels, as Menander and Marcus hold, even if it were the construction of some fiery being, likewise an angel, as Apelles teaches, the patronage of a secondary divinity would suffice for the authority of the flesh. We know angels [as coming] next after God. Even now, whoever that supreme god of any heretic may be, I would not unjustly derive the dignity of the flesh from him too, since the will to produce it was present with him.
passages.notes: "Marco": the manuscripts are uncertain here; some editors read Saturnino, and Marcus (the Valentinian) is not certain.
